learningObjective: Distinguish end-to-end latency from microbenchmark latency and identify when a microbenchmark speedup does not translate to end-to-end speedup.

canonicalClaims.claim: End-to-end speedup follows Amdahl's law: it is bounded above by 1 / ((1-f) + f/k), where f is the fraction of end-to-end time spent in the optimized op and k is the microbenchmark speedup. A large k with small f yields a small end-to-end improvement.
conditions: The optimization affects only the target op's execution time.
The rest of the pipeline is unchanged.
nonImplications: Does not imply small end-to-end gains are unimportant at scale.
Does not imply Amdahl is the only constraint; cross-op memory traffic and batch effects matter too.

misconceptions.claim: Kernel-level speedup composes multiplicatively into end-to-end speedup.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Amdahl weights speedup by time fraction; a small-fraction op cannot dominate.

misconceptions.claim: Fusing an op amplifies its end-to-end speedup via downstream cache reuse.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Cross-op cache reuse can help slightly but rarely converts a small time fraction into a large end-to-end share.

misconceptions.claim: Launch overhead subtracts from end-to-end speedup linearly.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Launch overhead is a fixed CPU cost, not a linear subtraction from GPU speedup.

misconceptions.claim: End-to-end and kernel-level speedups are equivalent when the kernel is called many times.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Number of calls does not remove the Amdahl weighting by time fraction.
